notes: Libel summary judgment appeal on qualified privilege and express malice; Horrocks v Lowe analysis and outcome are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Placement report libel: summary judgment on qualified privilege
key_facts: Social work student Terry Meade brought a libel action over unfavourable feedback reports written by managers at the Carers' Centre, Oxford, for his Ruskin College placement.
The defendants applied to strike out the claim or for summary judgment on the basis that the reports were published on an occasion of qualified privilege.
The claimant pleaded express malice, relying partly on a talking doorknocker gift and alleged ulterior motives to sabotage his career.
Master Rose refused summary judgment; the defendants appealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a master's refusal to strike out a libel claim or grant summary judgment for the defendants.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; summary judgment entered for the defendants; master's permission to rely on additional pleaded material set aside.
enrichment.ratio: Feedback reports prepared under a duty between placement provider, practice teacher and college were published on an occasion of qualified privilege; on the pleaded and assumed facts there was no real prospect of proving express malice because there was no evidence the defendants did not honestly believe what they wrote, and a spiteful gift did not make dishonest reporting more likely.
legal_issues: Whether placement feedback reports were published on an occasion of qualified privilege
Whether the claimant had a real prospect of proving express malice
Whether a jury could properly find malice on the pleaded evidence
Whether additional material in a respondent's notice should be admitted on appeal

notes: Compulsory purchase compensation appeal; rule (2) versus rule (6) analysis under the 1961 Act is detailed and conclusive.

enrichment.short_title: Compulsory purchase: no separate compensation for lost developer profit
key_facts: Ryde International owned 37 flats and 5 bungalows in Croydon compulsorily acquired by London Regional Transport for the Croydon Tramlink scheme.
The Lands Tribunal valued the property on a hypothetical single-sale basis, deducting developer profit, risk and finance costs.
Ryde argued it should also recover lost development profit separately under rule (6) because it would otherwise have sold units individually over time.
The tribunal initially accepted a separate rule (6) claim but later reversed itself.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a Lands Tribunal decision on market value compensation under the Land Compensation Act 1961.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no separate compensation payable under rule (6) for lost developer profit; tribunal award confirmed.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 5 rule (2) open market value is assessed on a hypothetical sale at the valuation date, commonly to an entrepreneur purchaser; a deduction for profit reflects risk and does not require separate compensation under rule (6), because acquisition replaces expected profit with a statutory debt and interest, and any additional value from separate marketing would be directly based on land value and excluded by rule (6).
legal_issues: Whether lost developer profit is compensatable under section 5 rule (6)
How developer profit deductions in residual valuations relate to the principle of equivalence
Whether rule (2) assumes a single sale or individual unit sales
Whether Mallick v Liverpool City Council supports a separate profit claim

notes: Major parallel-import trademark appeal with ECJ reference deferred on co-branding and de-branding; first-instance necessity findings upheld but final packaging issues remain open.

enrichment.short_title: Pharmaceutical parallel imports: reboxing necessity upheld, ECJ reference on packaging
key_facts: Pharmaceutical manufacturers sued parallel importers Swingward and Dowelhurst for reboxing, relabelling, co-branding and partial de-branding of genuine medicines imported from other EU member states.
Laddie J referred questions to the ECJ and, after its answers, held reboxing necessary but co-branding and de-branding unlawful.
Jacob LJ upheld findings that strong consumer resistance to overstickered packs made reboxing necessary to achieve effective market access.
The court deferred final rulings on packaging forms and referred further questions because of conflicting national court approaches.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals and cross-appeals from Laddie J's judgments following an ECJ reference on pharmaceutical parallel import repackaging.
enrichment.outcome: Cross-appeals on passing off and notice injunction dismissed; necessity to rebox upheld; judgment deferred on co-branding, de-branding and stickering pending further ECJ reference; 15 working days held appropriate BMS notice period.
enrichment.ratio: Replacement packaging is objectively necessary where, without repackaging, effective access to a substantial part of the market is hindered by strong resistance from a significant proportion of consumers to relabelled pharmaceuticals; however, whether co-branding or partial de-branding exceeds what is necessary, and the financial consequences of inadequate BMS notice, remain doubtful points requiring ECJ guidance.
legal_issues: Whether reboxing parallel imported pharmaceuticals is necessary under Bristol-Myers Squibb conditions
Whether co-branding or de-branding repackaging can be restrained as unnecessary
Whether Boehringer's passing off claim over generic-name boxes succeeds
What notice period satisfies BMS condition 5
Whether relabelling form must meet a necessity test

notes: Secure tenancy possession appeal for antisocial behaviour by tenant's son; suspension discretion analysis is straightforward.

enrichment.short_title: ASB secure tenancy possession: immediate order substituted for suspension
key_facts: New Charter Housing sought possession of a secure tenancy at 2 Hus Street, Droylsden, occupied by Ruth Ashcroft.
Her 17-year-old son Damon committed prolonged antisocial behaviour on the estate, breaching interim and final ASBOs and receiving a six-month detention order.
Witnesses left the estate through fear; the tenant failed to control Damon and threatened reprisals if evicted.
The judge made a possession order suspended for 12 months; the landlord appealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Landlord's appeal against a suspended possession order under Housing Act 1988 Schedule 2 ground 14.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; suspended order set aside; possession ordered in six weeks.
enrichment.ratio: Where ground 14 is made out against a tenant for a child's persistent nuisance, suspension is inappropriate if the tenant has shown no intention to control the child, further breach is likely, and witness intimidation makes future enforcement doubtful; a last opportunity to demonstrate reform is not a sufficient basis for suspension.
legal_issues: Whether a tenant may be dispossessed for nuisance caused by an uncontrollable child
Whether the judge mis exercised discretion in suspending possession for 12 months
Relevance of ASBO breach and witness attrition to suspension
Comparison with Camden City Council v Lowe

notes: Short EPA duty-of-care appeal on meaning of escape; statutory interpretation and outcome are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Waste duty of care: deliberate dumping is not 'escape' under section 34
key_facts: Gateway Professional Services was convicted of failing to prevent escape of controlled waste under section 34(1)(b).
An employee deliberately deposited black bags of commercial office waste on neighbouring land contrary to company instructions.
The magistrates accepted instructions had been given but convicted because monitoring was inadequate.
The company appealed by case stated on whether deliberate depositing amounted to escape from control.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated against magistrates' conviction under section 34(1)(b) of the Environmental Protection Act 1990.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction quashed; magistrates erred in law; question answered in the affirmative.
enrichment.ratio: Escape of waste under section 34(1)(b) means accidental spillage, leakage or loss of control, not deliberate deposit on another's land; deliberate dumping is properly prosecuted under section 33(1)(a) or section 34(1)(a), and section 34(1)(b) did not fit the facts.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'escape of waste from his control' in section 34(1)(b)
Whether deliberate dumping can constitute escape
Relationship between sections 33 and 34 of the Environmental Protection Act 1990
Relevance of the statutory Code of Practice on duty of care

notes: Planning section 288 challenge to inspector's refusal; policy S30 interpretation and reasons challenge both rejected clearly.

enrichment.short_title: Castle Terrace planning appeal: policy S30 bars garden plot dwelling
key_facts: Whiteknights Consultants Ltd sought planning permission for a dwelling and garage on garden land split from 36 Castle Terrace, Berwick-upon-Tweed.
The garden plot was subdivided and sold in 1994; local plan policy S30 adopted in 1999 prohibits subdivision of garden ground for new dwellings in Castle Terrace.
Northumberland refused permission; an inspector dismissed the appeal by written representations.
The claimants argued policy S30 did not apply because subdivision occurred before adoption and that precedent and PPG3 favoured permission.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 application to quash an inspector's dismissal of a planning appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; inspector's decision upheld; permission to appeal refused; costs summarily assessed at £3,000.
enrichment.ratio: Local plan policy S30 is concerned with development—construction of a new dwelling on subdivided garden ground—not with the prior act of subdivision itself; once properly construed, the 1994 split was immaterial and the inspector lawfully refused permission to avoid precedent erosion despite PPG3 and design merits.
legal_issues: Whether policy S30 applies where garden land was subdivided before policy adoption
Purposive construction of local plan policies against the statutory development control framework
Whether the inspector failed to consider material considerations under section 54A
Adequacy of reasons for rejecting precedent and PPG3 arguments
linked_authorities: Save Britain's Heritage v No. 1 Poultry Ltd [1991] 1 WLR 153

confidence.notes: Policy construction and inspector reasoning are thoroughly explained; costs discussion is peripheral.

notes: Split Court of Appeal on VAT betting exemption for call-centre agent; Arden LJ would refer to ECJ while Jacob and Auld LJJ would dismiss as acte clair.

enrichment.short_title: VAT exemption for betting agents: split court on Article 13B(f)

statutes_considered.title: EC Sixth Council Directive on VAT 77/388/EEC

key_facts: Vertex, within a United Utilities VAT group, provided call-centre and IT services to Littlewoods for the Bet Direct telephone betting business.
Vertex staff accepted bets according to Littlewoods' Telebet parameters but did not set odds, handle money, or decide non-standard bets.
The tribunal and High Court held Vertex supplied standard-rated call-centre services outside the betting exemption.
On appeal the Commissioners conceded agents might qualify if Community law so required, but disputed whether Vertex performed an essential betting function.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against tribunal and High Court decisions that Vertex's services to Littlewoods were standard-rated for VAT.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed by majority; Jacob and Auld LJJ held exemption unavailable; Arden LJ would have referred to the ECJ; leave to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Administrative call-centre services that merely communicate Littlewoods' acceptance of bets according to preset criteria are not themselves the provision of facilities for placing bets under Article 13B(f); the exemption covers the gambling framework supplied by the bookmaker, not outsourced mechanical acceptance, and section 47(3) does not assist an agent supplying services to its principal.
legal_issues: Whether Article 13B(f) exempts betting agents who consummate wagers on a bookmaker's behalf
Whether communicating bet acceptance is an essential betting service
Applicability of financial services agent cases such as SDC and CSC Financial Services
Whether Community law is acte clair or requires an ECJ reference

notes: Criminal appeal on vacating guilty pleas after confiscation warning; discretion analysis is concise and definitive.

enrichment.short_title: Trade mark guilty pleas: no vacation for undisclosed confiscation risk
key_facts: Trading standards seized thousands of counterfeit mobile phone facias and batteries traced to Nadia Traders Ltd, run by Saqeb, Junaid and Hafeez Sheikh.
All three pleaded guilty to section 92(1)(c) possession counts; conspiracy and sale counts lay on the file.
After a restraint order indicating possible £11m confiscation proceedings, they applied to vacate their pleas.
Judge Khayat refused; the single judge granted leave to appeal only on whether non-disclosure of confiscation risk invalidated the pleas.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal to allow withdrawal of guilty pleas to trade mark offences.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; judge's refusal to vacate pleas upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to warn defendants before guilty pleas that confiscation proceedings might follow does not vitiate an otherwise informed and voluntary admission of guilt; confiscation is peripheral to whether the plea represented a genuine acknowledgment of guilt, and the discretion to change plea must be exercised sparingly.
legal_issues: Whether non-disclosure of possible confiscation proceedings justifies vacating guilty pleas
Scope of residual discretion to withdraw unequivocal guilty pleas
Whether confiscation risk affects the genuineness of admissions of guilt

notes: Homelessness judicial review on suitability of temporary accommodation; statutory guidance and mandatory relief are clearly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Homelessness duty: unsuitable B&B and hostel temporary accommodation
key_facts: The claimant, a disabled mother, and her 16-year-old son Liam were accepted as homeless in priority need by Southwark in December 2001.
Liam could not live in Southwark and needed his own bedroom; he was placed in care because temporary accommodation had only one room.
From 2001 to 2003 the claimant remained in unsuitable bed and breakfast accommodation; later offers included a cramped Croydon bedsit and a two-room Lewisham hostel.
Southwark argued its duty was discharged by the Lewisham offer; the claimant sought suitable two-bedroom self-contained temporary accommodation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim challenging suitability of temporary accommodation provided under section 193(2) of the Housing Act 1996.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; mandatory order requiring suitable two-bedroom self-contained temporary accommodation within two months; claimant awarded costs.
enrichment.ratio: Temporary accommodation must be suitable under section 206; where a child requires a separate bedroom and the family has already endured prolonged bed and breakfast placement, further hostel or single-room accommodation is unsuitable, and a local authority cannot discharge its section 193 duty by offering hostel rooms after years of inadequate temporary housing.
legal_issues: Whether bed and breakfast and hostel accommodation was suitable temporary housing
Effect of Homelessness Code of Guidance and 2003 Suitability Order on B&B use
Whether Southwark discharged its section 193 duty by later offers
Appropriate remedy where long-term unsuitable temporary accommodation has been provided
linked_authorities: R (Khan) v London Borough of Newham [2001] EWCA Admin 589

confidence.notes: Statutory framework, suitability findings, and mandatory relief are comprehensively explained.

notes: Traveller trespass radius possession order appeal; jurisdiction and evidence threshold analysis is detailed and unanimous.

enrichment.short_title: Traveller trespass: radius possession order set aside for insufficient evidence
key_facts: Travellers including Angela Drury unlawfully occupied Fermyn Woods near Corby in April 2003.
The landowner sought a possession order against persons unknown covering Fermyn Woods and 30 other separate woodlands within a 20-mile radius.
Evidence showed prior trespass history on various Forestry Commission woodlands but no link between occupants of Fermyn Woods and the other sites for over three years.
The judge granted the full radius order without reasons beyond general trespass history.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a possession order against trespassers under CPR Part 55 extending beyond the occupied woodland.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; order for possession limited to Fermyn Woods; radius extension to 30 other woodlands set aside.
enrichment.ratio: A possession order against trespassers may include separate land not yet occupied only on principles analogous to a quia timet injunction, requiring convincing evidence of real danger of imminent trespass on that land; propinquity and similarity alone, without evidence linking the current occupiers to other sites, are insufficient.
legal_issues: Whether the court may include unoccupied land in a possession order against trespassers
Criteria for 'radius orders' in Forestry Commission traveller cases
Relationship between possession orders and quia timet injunctions
What evidence links current trespassers to anticipated decampment elsewhere
